title: Marsanne
description: A full-bodied Rhône white of honey, almond and pear, often with Roussanne, and capable of long ageing.
L: Marsanne gives full-bodied whites with pear, quince, honeysuckle, almond and, with age, honey and nuts. Acidity is low to medium, alcohol moderate to high, texture waxy and rich. It's less aromatic than Viognier, more about texture than perfume.

Marsanne takes its name from the village of Marsanne, near Montélimar in the Rhône. It's a northern Rhône grape, closely linked to Roussanne, its frequent blending partner. It's more productive and reliable than Roussanne, but can be flabby if overcropped or picked too late.
Marsanne is full-bodied and waxy, more about texture than aroma.

Look for medium lemon to gold colour, a subtle nose of pear, almond and flowers, and a full, waxy palate with low to moderate acidity. Young, it can seem quiet; with age, it develops honey and nutty notes. Compared with Viognier, it's less perfumed and less apricot.
Marsanne is more aromatic than Viognier.
Not true. Viognier is far more perfumed. Marsanne is about texture.
Marsanne gives pear, almond and a waxy texture
It's named after a Rhône village and pairs with Roussanne
It's subtle young and honeyed with age

Marsanne is the main white grape of the northern Rhône's Hermitage, Crozes-Hermitage, Saint-Joseph and Saint-Péray, where it also makes sparkling wine. It's often blended with Roussanne, which adds aroma, acidity and finesse. In the south, it appears in Côtes du Rhône blends.

Roussanne, its partner, has russet skins, from roux, and gives more aromatic, herbal, elegant wines, with better acidity. But it's harder to grow, prone to disease and irregular yields. Marsanne gives body and reliability; Roussanne gives perfume and freshness. Together they make balanced blends.
Marsanne for body; Roussanne for freshness
Match each grape to its contribution.
Rhône whites are built from complementary grapes.

Australia's Victoria has some of the world's oldest Marsanne vines, at Tahbilk, in the Nagambie Lakes, planted in 1927. Tahbilk's Marsanne is unoaked, lean and citrus when young, turning honeyed and toasty after 10 years. It shows how well Marsanne can age.
Where are some of the oldest Marsanne vines in the world?
Marsanne leads the whites of Hermitage and Saint-Joseph
A white that ages for decades

Hermitage is a single granite hill above Tain-l'Hermitage, facing south. About a quarter of its wine is white, mostly Marsanne with some Roussanne. The granite and loess, with full southern sun, give rich, powerful whites. Chapoutier and Jean-Louis Chave are famous producers.

White Hermitage is rich and fruity when young, then often closes up for several years, from about year 3 to 10, showing little aroma. After that, it opens again with honey, nuts, beeswax and dried fruit. The best can age 20 to 50 years, despite modest acidity, thanks to their concentration and phenolics.
White Hermitage often goes through a closed, quiet phase before opening again with age.
Yes. Many go quiet for several years, then develop honey and nutty complexity.

Producers make white Hermitage in different ways: some ferment and age in oak barrels for richness; others use old wood or steel to keep purity. Some sweet vin de paille, from dried grapes, is made in tiny amounts. Crozes-Hermitage whites are lighter and more affordable.
Oaked or pure; sweet vin de paille
Why can white Hermitage age for decades?
Its acidity is modest; concentration and phenolic structure carry it.
White Hermitage is mostly Marsanne from a granite hill
It often closes up, then reopens with honey and nuts

Marsanne's body and texture suit rich dishes: roast chicken, veal in cream sauce, lobster, crab, scallops, and dishes with butter or almonds. Aged white Hermitage suits truffle, mushrooms and hard cheeses like Comté. Avoid very acidic or very spicy food.

Serve at 11 to 13 degrees, not too cold. Simple Marsanne is good young. White Hermitage is best either within two to three years or after ten. Tahbilk's aged Marsanne shows how unoaked versions develop too.
Which dish suits an aged white Hermitage?
Rich, earthy dishes match its honeyed, nutty development.
Decant an older white Hermitage. Like a red, it benefits from air, opening its nutty, honeyed aromas.
Acidic dressings make low-acid wines taste flat.
Marsanne suits lobster, veal and Comté
Drink white Hermitage young or after ten years
What does Roussanne add to Marsanne?
Marsanne connects the Rhône and Victoria.
Marsanne is known for intense, explosive aromas.
Not true. It's subtle, more about texture.
Its acidity is low to medium.
